author: Pinxter Analytics
title: A lot of noise has come out in recent weeks about repatriati
text:
A lot of noise has come out in recent weeks about repatriation and what it might mean for investors. As I highlighted in my recent article about Apple's (NASDAQ: AAPL ) repatriation realities Apple: Don't Get Your Hopes Up in more detail, some companies simply don't have the capacity or the desire to return all their oversees cash given certain market dynamics and the relatively high (historically based) repatriation tax rate the current tax bill entails.
The two companies that garner the most attention are Apple and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT ) since their cash piles are among the largest held oversees with a combined value of around $400 billion, held mostly in Ireland and Asia. As vast amounts of speculation on what the two tech behemoths might do with that cash once it's taxed the mandatory repatriation rate, most key aspects of amounts and desires for use have been incorrectly stated, causing most outcomes to be on the verge of ludicrous.
Repatriation: The Actual Tax A lot of numbers have been floated around without much regard to what the actual law entails. The current headlines numbers for a mandatory repatriation are 15.5% on all liquid assets, no questions asked.
However, taxes already paid by any corporation on the aforementioned cash held (retained earnings) is considered paid and will not be subject to an additional tax, as stated in the tax code:

Subject to certain limitations, U.S. citizens, resident individuals, and domestic corporations are allowed to claim credit for foreign income taxes they pay. A domestic corporation that owns at least 10 percent of the voting stock of a foreign corporation is allowed a "deemed-paid" credit for foreign income taxes paid by the foreign corporation that the domestic corporation is deemed to have paid when the related income is distributed as a dividend or is included in the domestic corporation's income under the anti-deferral rules. 
''If a domestic corporation chooses to have the benefits of subpart A of part III of subchapter N (redacted) for any taxable year, an amount equal to the taxes deemed to be paid by such corporation under subsections (A), (B) and (D) of section 960 (determined without regard to the phrase '80 percent of' in subsection) for such taxable year shall be treated for purposes of this title as a dividend received by such domestic corporation from the foreign corporation.''
